description:
Team AWACS combined clinical, pharmacy, business analysis, and software skills for astronaut health monitoring.

Noor (Medical Analyst) and Rahaf (Pharmacy Analyst) supplied prioritised user stories and clinical review to keep the tool safe and non-diagnostic. Brett (Business Analyst) structured requirements, prioritisation, and UAT across time zones. Jude (IT Developer) built the FreeBruff dashboard and Python/FastAPI layer with ranked alerts, baseline comparison, body map, and offline support.
summary:
AWACS is a local-first health monitoring dashboard system that helps astronauts assess their own status and take clear next steps when Earth contact is delayed. 

It ranks alerts (Act Now / Monitor / Routine), shows the data that triggered each alert against the astronaut’s personal baseline, and gives simple guidance for non-physicians — all while working fully offline.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

AWACS is a wellness dashboard system that helps astronauts answer three questions in seconds: What changed? How far is it from my normal? What should I consider next?

It compares live readings with each astronaut's personal baseline and ranks alerts as Act Now (red), Monitor (yellow) or Routine (green). Tapping an alert shows the data that triggered it, the threshold, and the gap from the astronaut's baseline. A colour-coded body map shows status with a short reason for each zone, and a radiation panel puts shelter guidance at the top when needed. Core functions are designed to keep working offline during communication delays. AWACS supports wellness only. It does not diagnose or prescribe.

What benefits does it have?

Instead of relying on a single sensor, AWACS uses Triple Modular Redundancy: it compares three independent readings and uses majority agreement to spot outliers. This helps crews and mission support tell a possible health concern from a possible equipment fault, so they can make better-informed decisions far from Earth.

What is the intended impact?

We aim to support safer space exploration by giving astronauts and mission teams a clear view of crew health, with redundant sensor checks flagging potentially unreliable readings. Our proof of concept is not integrated with NASA's systems. Long term, we would like to explore compatibility with the Crew Health Care System (CHeCS) and contribute ideas to the Crew Health and Performance (CHP) framework, starting by understanding their technical requirements.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

A Python/FastAPI back end handles the baseline and anomaly logic, and a Framer type front end delivers the interactive interface. Multiple Superintelligence models included Grok, ChatGPT, Meta AI, Perplexity and Claude. As Business Analyst I ran the project through the usual BA tools - Jira, Confluence and Slack and Zoom for coms.

How is your project creative?

Rather than just displaying vital signs, AWACS communicates how much confidence to place in them and flags potential sensor faults. It is designed as one consistent experience across smartwatches, tablets, laptops and shared display boards. Our demo shows it in three settings: an ISS-like space station, a Moon base and a Mars base.

What factors did your team consider?

Clinical and pharmacy experts supplied and prioritised user stories and reviewed our prototype. These shaped our focus on patient safety, clear and actionable information, medication traceability, and separating a potential health concern from unreliable sensor data. We also considered usability across devices and operation without a live connection to Earth. The user stories describe our intended capabilities, not a claim that every feature is implemented or clinically validated. Two examples:

  • As an astronaut, I want each alert to show its triggering readings, threshold and baseline difference, so I understand why it appeared.
  • As a crew medical officer, I want inconsistent sensor readings flagged, so I can investigate a possible equipment fault before relying on the data.
